newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 2.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. -- BUDGET 'TO CUT DEFICIT OVER 5 YEARS'

The summer Budget due to be announced Wednesday by Chancellor Gordon Brown is expected to be introduced as a 'five-year deficit reduction plan'. The Budget, the first to be produced by a Labour government for 18 years, is likely to include a rise in net taxes in the current year of more than 2 billion stg, and significantly bigger increases in succeeding years. Brown is expected to introduce a sharp rise in the duty on petrol and the abolition of the 20 percent tax credit on dividend payments.
-- EUROTUNNEL OFFERED LONGER LICENCE DEAL

Eurotunnel, the troubled operator of the Channel Tunnel, has secured provisional agreement from the British and French governments for an extension to its operating concession from 65 to at least 99 years. The heavily-indebted company has been involved in a two-year stand-off with the governments over the issue of the concession period. If a deal is concluded, it would boost the prospects that the company's 8.5-billion stg financial restructuring will be approved.
-- US REGULATOR APPROVES BOEING-MCDONNELL MERGER

The proposed 8-billion stg merger of US aerospace companies Boeing and McDonnell-Douglas has been approved by the American regulator, the Federal Trade Commission. The FTC nodded through the merger without conditions, although it warned that it intends to monitor the potential anti-competitive effects of exclusive long-term contracts. The merger has still to be approved by the European Commission, which is due to give its verdict on July 23.
-- KOHL HARDENS DECIMAL DEBATE LINE

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has ruled out a fudge -- even by a tenth of one percentage point -- of the public sector deficit criteria for the planned European single currency. The move follows intense pressure from conservative coalition partners in Bavaria. Speaking in Munich, Kohl also gave the strongest signal yet that Germany's official debt would be converted into the euro at the scheduled start date of economic and monetary union.
-- BRUSSELS PLANS HORMONES APPEAL

The European Commission is planning to appeal after a confidential report from the World Trade Organisation backed complaints from Canada and the US that a European Union ban on imports of hormone-treated beef is unfair and illegal. The Commission said the ruling could have far-reaching implications for consumer protection, and it was greeted with dismay by European consumer and farming groups.
-- BRUSSELS MEETING LEAVES BA-AA ALLIANCE STALLED

Margaret Beckett, the UK trade and industry secretary, met with European competition commissioner Karel van Miert on Tuesday to discuss the controversial proposed alliance between British Airways and Amerian Airlines. The central issues of debate at the meeting were how many slots the allied group would be permitted to operate at Heathrow airport and the frequencies of flights.
-- WOOLWICH SIGNALS PAYBACK

UK building society Woolwich, which is set to float on the stock market on Monday, converting it into a five-bn stg bank, has indicated that it will return some of its excess capital to new shareholders. Due to high prices and increased competition among bidders, Woolwich has also played down suggestions that it is seeking big acquisitions in the UK. Woolwich chief executive John Stewart hopes that the group will be able to begin handing back capital at the annual meeting next spring.
-- MFI SALES CAST DOUBT ON CONSUMER BOOM

Furniture manufacturer MFI has reported a slow-down in sales growth, prompting some analysts to question the widespread belief that Britain is experiencing a consumer boom. New sales at the group were up five percent in the first nine months of the year and sales were described as generally being 'flat'.
-- PEARSON SELLS TROLL STAKE

Media, entertainment and leisure group Pearson has sold its 49 percent stake in Troll Communications for $92 million to Canada's Torstar Corporation. Torstar is now in possession of the entire Troll company. The sell-off signals a further departure from the world of children's book distribution for Pearson, which originally acquired the Troll Stake in 1995 for $59 million.
-- MEDICAL RESEARCH FACES SKILLS SHORTAGE THREAT

A taskforce set up by the Committee of Vice-Chancellors and Principals has warned that the future of Britain's university medical departments as centres of world-class research is threatened by a severe shortage of clinical academics. According to a report from the group, the shortage could affect the National Health Service and the UK's thriving pharmaceutical industry because university-based clinical academics are vital for training and research.
